newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Jaguar new car could be built overseas.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Jaguar new car could be built overseas.

text.p: Jaguar's foray into the smaller luxury car market could well be a success, but analysts warned on Wednesday that pressure to build the X400 model abroad could tarnish its image as a pedigree British car-maker.
A debate is currently raging between Jaguar Cars Ltd and its U.S. parent Ford Motor Co over where to build the X400.

Analysts were betting that Ford would win the argument to build overseas on the grounds of cheaper costs. The issue will be decided as part of a three month feasibility study currently underway, which could double output to 200,000 by the year 2000.
But a warning came from some analysts that moves to cut costs by moving production abroad could backfire on the brand.
"If it's not built in Britain, it could be a marketing disaster. The loss of potential sales could be up to 25 percent," said Arthur Maher, head of European research at LMC International.
A likely possibility would be to use an existing Ford car-building platform, which would be cheaper than building a new plant, which would be another option.

Despite that danger, the large-volume X400 car, seen selling around 100,000 units, is expected to compete well in an already fiercely competitive sector which includes the BMW-3 Series, the Mercedes C-Class and the Audi A4, said analysts.
"They will have no difficulty with 100,000 in sales," said John Lawson, at Salomon Brothers.
Jaguar's move to broaden its product base which follows other luxury car-makers.
Analysts see substantial growth potential despite the raging debate over where to build the new X400.
Jaguar confirmed a debate was on over whether to take production for the new X400 overseas -- a move backed by its Ford parent, which is currently in the throes of a European cost-cutting programme.

Colin Cook, spokesman for Jaguar admitted it already had capacity constraints at its British plants in Coventry and Castle Bromwich in central England, indicating that switching to a foreign plant may be necessary.
"It would be very difficult to expand our existing plants and we would not build a new plant in Britain," he told Reuters.
"The feasibility study will be international in scope and overseas locations are being looked at. There has been speculation about Germany and the U.S," Cook said.
Another factor likely to weigh in favour of an overseas production base for the X400 is the value of the strong pound, which bumps up British based export prices. "Sterling is a factor," said Cook.
But some warned that if the X400 is built overseas and possibly based on a Ford Mondeo platform, which is likely, this could impact on Jaguar's British brand name and sales.
"We think it will be based on a Mondeo platform," said Arthur Maher, head of European research at LMC International, sister firm to U.S. analyst JD Power.
"Customers will say 'Why should I pay a premium for a Jaguar when it's a rebadged Scorpio or Mondeo?' Jaguar may have to reflect this in the X400 margins."
Lawson, analyst at Salomon Brothers, agreed production could be moved abroad, but said the impact may not be so painful.

"Remember Mercedes is no longer just built in Germany any more, the same with BMW, even Porsche's Boxter. I think these examples encouraged Ford to consider overseas production. As long as the quality is right it could work."
The X400 will be Jaguar's smallest car and will follow the launch of the X200 -- a mid-sized car -- in 1999. The Jaguar range currently consists of the large XJ saloons and the XK8 sports car.
Maher said the decision to invest "hundreds of millions of pounds" in another new model marked Ford's confidence in Jaguar's turnaround from years of losses.
"The bottom line in Jaguar is finally paying off after the disaster period which followed the takeover." Ford paid $2.5 billion for Jaguar in 1989.
